doc.title: Jack Palmer interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 24, 1997

chapter: Back in New York, circus and friends
title: Standing on the corner in New York, pay and the union transfer
summary: After the war he stood with his trumpet on 48th Street, took a Brooklyn dance job for about fifteen to twenty dollars, and waited out the union transfer.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: Were you able to get back into music full time after World War II?

Oh, well, I just packed up myself, and I went to New York. And I checked in some apartment building and then I stood on a corner with my trumpet case. Somebody came up and tapped me and said, “Want to play Saturday night? Are you working Saturday?” I said, “No.”
Is that right? And you didn’t know this person?

No. Well there were two corners to stand on. On the corner of 48th Street and Broadway, and 52nd Street and Broadway. But 52nd Street was high class musicians. 48th Street was a lower class. Well what I mean, on 52nd Street, they were in radio at the time, it wasn’t television. And the guys up there did recording dates and so forth. Down here we just did saloons and — oh boy, starving days.
Yeah?
Oh.
Paying your dues, huh? So this guy came up and hired you for a dance?
Where was that?
On 48th Street, you’re standing on the corner.
Oh, yeah.
And this guy comes up and just asks—

I had the trumpet — you always walked around with your trumpet case you know. “You working Saturday night?” I says, “No.” He says, “You want to work?” “Yeah.” “Well do you know Brooklyn at all?” I says, “Well I’ll find it, don’t worry, tell me what.” So he told me what the name of the place and how to get there, what trains to take you know, and I wrote things down, and I went there and I played that Saturday night. Well evidently they liked my playing because they took my name and phone number and said, “You want to work next Saturday?” I said, “Well I’ll see you Wednesday, and I’ll let you know, because I think I have something else I might have promised and I don’t want to” which I hadn’t. But I didn’t want to get into a steady Saturday night thing there, then I wouldn’t be free, you know what I mean? I still wanted to be available, that was the thing, was to be available for a better thing.
Because a job like that that you played with this guy, how much would that pay?
Oh at that time, gee, I think about eighteen dollars.
In New York City.

Yeah fifteen dollars maybe. If you got twenty like that was good. And twenty five was better, and thirty, wow — that was a wow, thirty. Oh boy. So the whole thing was I was © Fillius Jazz Archive -18-
on transfer then, so I couldn’t work a steady job in the first three months. You couldn’t work a steady job, even if it was offered.
You had to go through that whole thing again, coming back to New York?
Oh, yeah. But after three months I could accept a job, if I got one, with permission, a steady job.
Permission from the union rep or whatever?
